title: Webflow Pricing 2026: Plans, Seats, and Real Costs
summary: Webflow pricing structures vary significantly based on your specific traffic levels and required CMS features for your digital projects.
body_markdown:
## Webflow pricing plans and monthly costs for 2026


When you look at[Webflow](https://webflow.com/blog/pricing-updates-2022) ’s 2026 pricing, you are looking at a dual-subscription model where users must pay for both a Site plan to host content and a[Workspace](https://workspace.google.com/pricing) plan to manage the team.


Because of this decoupled structure, a single "Premium" site (formerly Business) costs $25 per month billed yearly or $39 monthly before any seats or add-ons, so the total rises once a designer seat is included.


### Webflow site plans for hosting and CMS pricing


Site plans function as your hosting and database license, scaling primarily on traffic volume and the number of items in your Content Management System (CMS). Under the 2026 billing structure, these infrastructure costs are separated from the people working on the site.


Between $15 and $60 per month is what you will pay for individual site hosting, while Workspace plans for team collaboration add another $19 to $49 per seat, which means your total monthly overhead scales significantly as your organization grows.


If you choose a DIY build,[The Hoop Studio](https://www.thehoopstudio.com/resources/insights/real-cost-diy-webflow-site-vs-hiring-studio) estimates your initial investment between 500 and 5,000 dollars. Even a "free" tool requires significant capital for templates and learning time.


Outsourcing to a Studio build pushes costs to a range of **9,000 to 50,000 dollars** , meaning the platform is no longer a budget alternative to custom development.


This is where high-performance sites usually land to accommodate growth, effectively capping your scaling potential at that specific threshold.


These base hosting rates reflect pure infrastructure before team management fees are applied.


The Premium hosting tier (formerly Business) costs $25 when billed annually or $39 on a month-to-month cycle, but operational add-ons quickly elevate these figures, so your final monthly invoice will almost certainly exceed the advertised starting price.


### Workspace plans for team collaboration


Workspace plans are the "seat tax" required for anyone who needs to edit the site’s structure or design. While a Starter workspace is free, it limits you to two unhosted sites, so you cannot stage multiple client projects simultaneously without upgrading.


Small marketing teams will find the Core plan at $19/mo billed yearly is the entry point for more staging, since every Workspace plan includes 1 full seat and you can purchase more.


Trustradius notes that for larger teams, the Growth plan at $49/mo billed yearly adds advanced permissions such as site-specific access.


You cannot restrict a junior designer from deleting the global CSS without paying a premium.


To safeguard layouts without adding expensive seats, Activepieces executes multi-step data validation workflows under a flat rate of 1 credit per flow run, no matter how many steps the process requires.


> You cannot restrict a junior designer from deleting the global CSS without paying a premium.


This ensures that breaking down complex Webflow updates into smaller, safer operational steps does not increase costs, bypassing the step-based penalties of Zapier's per-task billing and Make's per-module billing.


### E-commerce plans for digital storefronts


E-commerce plans bundle CMS hosting with transaction processing, but they carry a 2% transaction fee on the $29/mo Standard tier.


This means a store doing $10,000 in monthly sales pays an extra $200 in fees to Webflow, making it more expensive than dedicated platforms.


**The $74/mo Plus plan removes this transaction fee, so it becomes the mathematical break-even point once a store clears $2,250 in monthly volume.**


Once you reach the $212/mo Advanced tier, you gain a limit of 15,000 items.


On the Advanced tier, this is the only way to host a complex inventory without moving to an Enterprise contract, forcing a significant jump in overhead costs once you exceed that capacity.
